title: The last words in Pali
hookLine: a saved voicemail, a last text: the Buddha's last words, and two ways to hear them
tomorrow: dhamma or dharma: which spelling is the right one?

cards: Some people keep a voicemail for years because of what it is: the last thing someone said to them. Last words get weighed and replayed.

In the Digha Nikaya, the Buddha is lying between two sala trees at Kusinara, near the end. He asks his monks whether anyone has a doubt left, about the Buddha, the teaching, the path. He asks a second time, and a third.
Silence. Then he speaks. The text says plainly: these were his last words.
And ever since, people have heard them two ways.

teach.b: Here they are: vayadhamma sankhara, appamadena sampadetha. Vaya, falling away; dhamma, nature; sankhara, things put together. Whatever is put together has the nature to fall apart.
Then: appamadena, with appamada; sampadetha, bring it to completion. Rhys Davids gave it this way: "Decay is inherent in all component things! Work out your salvation with diligence!"
Salvation is his word; the Pali simply says bring it to completion. Now the debate, and it lives inside the tradition.
One side hears urgency. Things fall apart, the teacher is leaving, time is short: strive. Don't wait for a better year.
That reading has the first half on its side, and the ring of diligence.

teach.h: THE OTHER: CARE. DON'T GET CARELESS.
teach.b: The other side hears care. Appamada is a negative: not heedless, not careless, and the commentary ties it to mindfulness that never goes missing. Read that way, the last word isn't a whip.
It's a steady hand: pay attention, and keep paying it. That reading has the word itself on its side. Both sides chant the same line, and the line can carry both: the push and the attention.

how: Buddhists recall the Buddha's last words at Vesak and at memorials, and some teachers close a retreat or a talk with them, in Pali or in translation.

games.q: what does “the last words in pali” mean?
o: a funeral verse that monks chant over the dead body
final advice: things pass, so keep going with care
the Buddha's goodbye blessing to his own family

games.q: the last words — tap the pairs.
p: of the nature to fall away

s: the Pali of the last words says 'salvation'
salvation is Rhys Davids' word; sampadetha means bring to completion.
before speaking, the Buddha asked three times if anyone had a doubt
a first, a second and a third time; the monks were silent.
appamada just means working as hard as possible
it's a negative, not heedless, not careless; the commentary ties it to mindfulness.

games.q: your friend reads 'work out your salvation with diligence' and says it means grind until you drop. what's the best case for the other side?
o: appamada is heedfulness: steady attention that never goes missing, not a frantic push.
the last words were only a goodbye, so they don't really ask anything.
diligence is for monks; everyone else is meant to take it easy.
games.why: the care reading stands on the word itself, non-heedlessness, and the commentary's link to mindfulness. the urgency reading stands on 'things fall apart'. the line holds both.

practice: If you can, stand and walk slowly across the room and back for the sit. On one step, say inwardly vayadhamma sankhara; on the next, appamadena sampadetha.
If walking isn't possible, tap it out with your fingers on your knee, one phrase to each tap.

wordCard.voice: The last words in Pali: vayadhamma sankhara, appamadena sampadetha. Things fall apart; complete the path with care.

orig.note: Pali, in Devanagari letters: appamadena, with heedfulness; sampadetha, bring it to completion.

carryVoice: For the road: strive on with care, the push and the attention together. Until tomorrow.
